The whole plan, on your phone.

Most plastic advice is a wall of articles nobody finishes. This is ordered instead: the biggest sources of plastic in a typical home, arranged so the changes that cut your exposure most come first, each one paired with a swap that has actually been vetted.

There is a free option on every step, and it counts the same. Sometimes the best swap is something already in your kitchen. Paid picks appear only when they genuinely beat the free one.

And when you are standing in a shop wondering about something, you can get an answer before you buy rather than after. Search it by name, or scan the barcode if it is already in your hand, and see what it is made of, what it ships in, whether it was recalled, and what independent labs found.

No account to create, no ads, nothing sponsored. Every verdict is our own research rather than a brand telling you about itself.

Bottled water averages roughly 240,000 plastic particles per litre.

The detail that matters more than the number: most of them are nanoplastics. That is the fraction small enough to cross into tissue, and also the fraction almost no filter is tested against.

PET sheds into its own contents, and heat during shipping and storage makes it worse. A hot truck is part of the story.

Bamboo handle, plastic bristles.

The handle composts. The head does not. Almost every bamboo toothbrush on the shelf uses nylon bristles, and the bristles are the part that actually touches your mouth, twice a day, against your gums.

There is no clean natural alternative either. Boar bristle exists but holds bacteria and is not vegan. Nylon 4 and nylon 6 are marketed as biodegradable, but only under industrial composting conditions that most places do not have.

Which is not a reason to skip bamboo. It is a reason to know what you are actually buying, and to pull the bristles before composting the handle.

Certification has not caught up to the particles that matter most.

NSF 401 certifies a filter against microplastics. There is no equivalent standard for nanoplastics, which is the size that actually crosses membranes.

Reverse osmosis works around this because it filters by pore size. The membrane does not care what the particle is called, so it captures well below the certified range. Physics rather than paperwork.
